clinicalPearls: Consider TSS in any acute febrile illness with diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension, and multi-organ involvement, even without an obvious focal infection source.
A retained tampon, nasal packing, surgical wound packing, or postpartum/post-surgical site should always be actively sought and removed as part of initial assessment.
Streptococcal TSS typically presents with a clear, severe, deep soft-tissue focus (necrotizing fasciitis or bacteremia) and is far more often bacteremic than the staphylococcal form.
Desquamation of the palms and soles is a late finding, occurring one to two weeks after illness onset, and should never be relied upon to make the initial diagnosis.
Hypotension plus involvement of three or more organ systems (renal, hepatic, hematologic, mucosal, CNS, muscular/GI) in a febrile diffuse-rash illness supports the syndromic diagnosis.
Early aggressive fluid resuscitation is often required because of profound capillary leak, and volume needs can be extreme in the first 24-48 hours.
Source control (removing foreign material, draining/debriding infected tissue) is as critical as antimicrobial therapy and delays worsen outcomes.
Blood cultures are frequently negative in staphylococcal TSS since the syndrome is toxin-mediated rather than driven by bloodstream invasion.
reference.pathophysiology: TSS results from exotoxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus (notably TSST-1) or by Streptococcus pyogenes acting as superantigens that bind directly to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the conventional antigen groove. This bypasses normal antigen processing and triggers massive, non-specific polyclonal T-cell activation with a resulting cytokine storm (IL-1, IL-2, TNF, interferon-gamma). The surge in inflammatory mediators produces capillary leak, vasodilation, hypotension, and secondary multi-organ dysfunction, explaining why the clinical picture can be severe even with a small, localized focus of infection or colonization.
additionalDifferentials: Kawasaki disease (especially in children with fever, rash, and mucosal changes)
Necrotizing fasciitis without full toxic shock physiology
Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsial infections
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) or Stevens-Johnson spectrum
Septic shock from another gram-negative or gram-positive source
nonInfectiousMimics: Systemic lupus erythematosus flare with vasculitic rash
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures (times two) — often negative in staphylococcal TSS but essential to identify streptococcal bacteremia and guide therapy
Wound, vaginal, or device-site cultures — to isolate toxin-producing S. aureus or S. pyogenes and confirm source
Complete metabolic panel with renal and hepatic function — documents multi-organ involvement required for diagnosis
Complete blood count with differential — assesses for thrombocytopenia and left shift
Creatine kinase — elevated with muscular involvement/myositis component
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, fibrinogen) — screens for evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation
Imaging (CT/MRI or bedside ultrasound) of suspected soft-tissue focus — evaluates for necrotizing infection requiring surgical debridement
Serologic/toxin studies where available — can support etiology in atypical or culture-negative presentations
redFlags: Refractory hypotension unresponsive to initial fluid resuscitation, suggesting need for vasopressors and ICU-level care
Rapidly spreading pain, swelling, or crepitus over a soft-tissue site raising concern for necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergent surgical exploration
Evolving coagulopathy or falling platelet count concerning for disseminated intravascular coagulation
Altered mental status or new organ dysfunction indicating rapid progression to multi-organ failure
Any retained foreign material (tampon, packing, prosthetic material) not yet identified or removed
pitfalls: Dismissing the diagnosis because blood cultures are negative — staphylococcal TSS is toxin-mediated and frequently culture-negative.
Waiting for classic desquamation before considering the diagnosis, which delays treatment since desquamation occurs late in the course.
Failing to perform a thorough examination for retained foreign bodies (vaginal, nasal, surgical) as the driving source.
Underestimating streptococcal TSS severity because the cutaneous findings can be subtler than staphylococcal disease despite higher mortality.
reference.prognosis: Staphylococcal TSS has a lower mortality (roughly a few percent) when recognized early and the source is controlled, whereas streptococcal TSS carries a substantially higher mortality, often cited around 30-70%, particularly when associated with necrotizing soft-tissue infection or bacteremia. Prompt source control, resuscitation, and antimicrobial therapy are the main determinants of outcome.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Staphylococcal Infections and Streptococcal Infections chapters (Toxic Shock Syndrome sections)
management: Immediate source control — remove any retained tampon, nasal or wound packing and debride or drain a necrotising soft-tissue focus

Combination antimicrobial therapy pairing a beta-lactam (an antistaphylococcal penicillin, or vancomycin where meticillin-resistant S. aureus is possible, with streptococcal cover) and a protein-synthesis-inhibiting agent such as clindamycin or linezolid to suppress toxin production
Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation for capillary-leak hypotension, with vasopressors and organ support in intensive care
Intravenous immunoglobulin for severe or streptococcal toxic shock syndrome to neutralise circulating superantigen
Monitor and support multi-organ dysfunction — renal, hepatic, respiratory and haematological, including evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation
Escalate early to critical care and surgical teams for refractory shock or necrotising infection

algorithms.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome Emergency Resuscitation and Source Control Pathway

steps.action: Patient presenting with abrupt fever (> 38.9 C), diffuse sunburn-like erythroderma, hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg), and signs of capillary leak or multiorgan involvement.

Examine entire body for foreign objects: immediately remove retained vaginal tampons, nasal packs, surgical dressings. Inspect surgical wounds and soft tissues for crepitus, edema, or necrotizing fasciitis.
Profound capillary leak requires massive crystalloid fluid resuscitation (often 10 to 15 L in first 24h). Early central line and arterial line placement; start norepinephrine for refractory shock.

Administer bactericidal cell-wall active agent (IV Vancomycin or Cefazolin/Nafcillin) PLUS Protein Synthesis Inhibitor for toxin suppression (IV Clindamycin 900 mg 8-hourly or IV Linezolid 600 mg 12-hourly).
Administer high-dose IVIg (1 to 2 g/kg) to neutralize circulating bacterial superantigens (TSST-1, SpeA/C).

rows.parameter: Parenteral, serious infection: sensitive to penicillin

cells.text: Penicillin G 4 mU q4h
Nafcillin or oxacillin 2 g q4h, cefazolin 2 g q8h, vancomycin 1 g q12h (b)
Fewer than 5% of isolates are sensitive to penicillin

rows.parameter: Parenteral, serious infection: sensitive to methicillin

cells.text: Nafcillin or oxacillin 2 g q4h
Cefazolin 2 g q8h (b), vancomycin 15 to 20 mg/kg q8 to 12h (b)

Penicillin-allergic patients can have a cephalosporin if the allergy was not anaphylactic or accelerated; desensitization to beta-lactams may be indicated in selected serious infections needing maximal bactericidal activity (for example prosthetic valve endocarditis (d)). Type A beta-lactamase may rapidly hydrolyze cefazolin and reduce efficacy in endocarditis. Vancomycin is a less effective option

rows.parameter: Parenteral, serious infection: resistant to methicillin

cells.text: Vancomycin 15 to 20 mg/kg q8 to 12h (b)

Daptomycin 6 mg/kg q24h (b,c) for bacteremia, endocarditis and complicated skin infections; linezolid 600 mg q12h (400 mg q12h for uncomplicated skin infections); quinupristin/dalfopristin 7.5 mg/kg q8h

Test sensitivity before using an alternative. Adjunctive drugs, used only with other antimicrobials: gentamicin 1 mg/kg q8h (b), rifampin 300 mg PO q8h, fusidic acid 500 mg q8h (not readily available in the United States). Higher daptomycin doses have been used in some serious infections. Quinupristin/dalfopristin is bactericidal against methicillin-resistant isolates unless the strain is resistant to erythromycin or clindamycin. Efficacy of adjunctive therapy is not well established in many settings. Linezolid and quinupristin/dalfopristin have in vitro activity against most VISA and VRSA strains. See footnote (d) for prosthetic-valve endocarditis

nodes.text: Abrupt fever, diffuse erythroderma and hypotension (systolic below 90 mmHg)
Retained tampon, packing or necrotising soft-tissue focus?
Emergency source control and surgical exploration of the focus
Blood cultures (two sets), wound cultures and creatine kinase
Multi-organ involvement with erythroderma and hypotension present?
Antistaphylococcal beta-lactam or vancomycin, plus clindamycin or linezolid
Review Kawasaki, scarlet fever and necrotising fasciitis
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation; vasopressors for refractory shock
High-dose IV immunoglobulin 1 to 2 g/kg for severe or streptococcal TSS
Monitor coagulation (DIC), renal, liver and lung function in ICU
